statement: The 1521 fall of Tenochtitlan must be modeled as multi-causal, not a simple "conquistadors won" narrative. Hernán Cortés's Spanish force was small (roughly 250-500 men at various points); the actual besieging army at the final assault included, per Matthew Restall's synthesis, on the order of ~200,000 indigenous allied warriors, principally Tlaxcalans and other groups with pre-existing grievances against Mexica imperial tribute demands, who used the Spanish as leverage in their own regional conflicts rather than as passive collaborators. A major smallpox epidemic (1520-1521) killed an estimated one-third to one-half of the Basin of Mexico's population, including emperor Cuitláhuac, crippling leadership continuity and military capacity at the decisive moment (regional Mesoamerican mortality estimates run 5-8 million, though exact epidemic-onset dating is itself contested among historians reconciling native vs. Spanish-derived chronologies). Restall's central historiographical intervention: the "small band of heroic Spaniards defeats an empire" narrative is a myth generated by later Spanish self-mythologizing (reinforced by William H. Prescott's 1843 History of the Conquest of Mexico); the actual conquest was a collaborative, decentralized, multi-year, multi-actor war substantially won by indigenous manpower plus disease, not Spanish military superiority — now mainstream consensus among conquest historians, not a fringe revision.

sources.citation: Restall, Matthew. Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest. Oxford University Press, 2003; updated ed. 2021.
sources.author: Matthew Restall

does_not_demonstrate: That a small Spanish force alone military defeated the Mexica empire, as opposed to a collaborative indigenous-allied siege compounded by a major smallpox epidemic
